title: Scan in the City, Cash on the Steppe: A Realistic Money Plan for Mongolia
summary: Ulaanbaatar runs on QR codes while the countryside still runs on tugrik cash. Here's how visitors can join Mongolia's QR ecosystem, dodge ATM fees, and plan cash for the steppe.
body_markdown:
You're at Narantuul Market in Ulaanbaatar, haggling over a camel wool blanket. You've agreed on a price, you reach for your card, and the vendor shakes her head and taps a laminated square zip-tied to the stall frame. A QR code. Behind you, a local pays for a sack of aaruul the same way, phone out, two seconds, done. You have a foreign debit card, a handful of dollars, and no way to scan anything. So she points you toward an ATM three aisles away, the one with the line.


That little moment sums up money in Mongolia better than any guidebook paragraph. The capital has quietly gone digital. The rest of the country has not. If you plan for only one of those realities, you'll either bleed ATM fees in the city or stand cashless in a ger camp wondering why your phone has no bars, let alone a payment app that works.


## There are two Mongolias, financially speaking


Ulaanbaatar is where roughly half the country lives, and its shops, cafes, restaurants, and market stalls have embraced QR payments with real enthusiasm. Walk down Peace Avenue and you'll see QR stickers at coffee shops, pharmacies, convenience stores, even tiny kiosks selling SIM cards. Locals pay with bank apps linked to networks like[QPay](https://moretapay.com/networks/qpay) , and the whole thing moves fast. Many places would genuinely rather you scan than hand over notes.


Then you leave the city. Head to Terelj, the Gobi, Khuvsgul Lake, anywhere a driver has to point the Land Cruiser at open steppe, and the picture flips completely. Ger camps, roadside guanz canteens, families selling airag by the track, the herder who fixes your tire: these are cash transactions, in tugrik, often with no mobile signal for miles. This is one of those places where


[cash still wins for small, offline payments](https://moretapay.com/blog/the-jeepney-and-tricycle-problem-why-cash-still-wins-over-qr-for-micro-fares)


, and no app is going to change that on this trip.


So the honest answer to "how do I pay in Mongolia" is: both ways, deliberately. QR in the city, cash on the steppe. The trick is not letting the cash half of that plan quietly eat your budget.


## Where the money leaks: ATMs and exchange counters


Mongolia has few internationally friendly payment options for visitors, which is exactly why most travelers default to the ATM. And the ATM is where the leaks start. Your home bank may charge you for the foreign withdrawal. The local machine may add its own fee on top. Withdrawal limits per transaction mean you repeat the whole exercise more often than you'd like, paying the fixed costs each time.


Then there's the exchange rate question. If a machine or card terminal ever offers to charge you in your home currency instead of tugrik, decline it. That convenience almost always comes with a worse rate baked in. Always choose to be charged in MNT and let the conversion happen on better terms.


One more practical note: tugrik comes in relatively small denominations, so a meaningful withdrawal turns into a satisfying but bulky brick of banknotes. If you've traveled in Laos you know the feeling, and


[your wallet wasn't designed for that currency either](https://moretapay.com/blog/laos-qr-payments-avoid-atm-fees-lao-qr-kip-2026-2026-10-12)


. Budget pocket space accordingly.


## The QR codes are everywhere. Can a visitor actually use them?


Here's the frustrating part. The QR stickers you see all over Ulaanbaatar are built for people with Mongolian bank accounts and local apps. As a visitor, you can't just download a Mongolian banking app, verify with a local ID you don't have, and start scanning. For years that meant foreigners watched the QR economy from the outside and kept feeding the ATM.


This is where Moreta Pay changes the math. You top up a wallet from your own bank at home (US bank via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or with an international card, in your own currency. Then, at that market stall or cafe, you scan the merchant's standard local QR code, the same one locals use. The app shows you the amount, the exchange rate, and the merchant's name before you confirm anything, converts from your wallet, and the merchant is paid instantly in tugrik. No Mongolian bank account, no guessing what rate you got, no foreign transaction fee surprise on next month's statement.


In practice, that means your city days in Ulaanbaatar, which might be most of your nights and meals, stop requiring cash at all. Coffee near Sukhbaatar Square, dinner, the pharmacy run for altitude headache tablets before your Khuvsgul trip, the supermarket stock-up before a Gobi tour: scan, check, confirm.


## How much cash you actually need, and when to get it


Once QR covers the city, your cash needs shrink to the countryside portion of your trip, and that's a number you can estimate instead of guess. Think about it per day in the field: meals at guanz canteens, small purchases from herder families, tips for drivers and guides, park entry fees at remote gates, the odd emergency buffer. Tour operators will usually tell you what's included so you can work out the rest.


A sensible sequence looks like this:


- **Before you arrive:**


top up your Moreta Pay wallet from home so you land ready to scan in Ulaanbaatar.


- **In the city, early in the trip:**


make one or two larger, planned ATM withdrawals in tugrik to cover your entire countryside stretch, rather than five small panicked ones. Fewer withdrawals, fewer fixed fees.


- **Break the big notes down:**


pay for something small in cash at a supermarket to get change. On the steppe, nobody wants to break your largest bill for a bowl of tsuivan.


- **On tour:**


spend cash, and don't count on signal. Anything that can wait until you're back in UB can go back on QR.


- **Back in the city:**


return to scanning, so you're not stuck re-exchanging leftover tugrik at the airport at a bad rate.


## A few Mongolia-specific habits worth copying


**Confirm before you pay, every time.**


Mongolian merchants are used to QR customers checking the screen. With Moreta Pay you'll see the merchant name and the converted amount before confirming, which is also your sanity check that the stall's sticker is really theirs.


**City taxis are their own world.**


Plenty of Ulaanbaatar rides are informal, a local driver who pulls over when you hold out your hand. Those are cash, agreed up front. App-based rides and marked taxis are more structured. Keep small notes for the informal ones.


**Online bookings count too.**


If you're arranging accommodation or travel on platforms that support QR-based online checkout, such as Trip.com or Agoda, the same wallet works there, which is handy when your foreign card gets declined by a local booking page.


**Naadam and holidays mean queues.**


If you're visiting in July for Naadam, ATMs near the stadium and in tourist areas get hammered. Doing your countryside cash withdrawal days earlier is a small move that saves real standing-around time.


Mongolia rewards travelers who plan in layers: digital where the country is digital, cash where it isn't, and no money wasted crossing between the two. Sort the QR half before your flight by


[setting up Moreta Pay and loading your wallet in your own currency](https://moretapay.com/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=country-seo)


, then save the ATM for the one job it still does best here: funding the steppe.
